prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, which brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are the strongest candidate on this shortlist on every test I apply as an experimentalist. Katori's magic-wavelength idea removes the light shift that would otherwise spoil spectroscopy of trapped atoms, and Ye's group turned it into the most accurate and stable measurement instrument ever demonstrated. The credit is clean: two names, one concept and its decisive realisation, both fully covered by the supplied names. The result is not a single claim awaiting confirmation. Several independent laboratories (JILA, Tokyo/RIKEN, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and others) operate and compare lattice clocks at or below 1e-17, which is the kind of independent confirmation I always ask for. The physics will last: it feeds the redefinition of the second, tests of constants and of relativistic redshift over millimetre height differences, and sensors for geodesy. It opens a new observational window through an instrument, and seven of eight members placed it on their ballot, four of them first.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is novelty relative to earlier prizes. Frequency combs (2005) and single-ion clocks and quantum control (2012) already honoured the neighbouring ground, and a committee could judge lattice clocks to be a very successful refinement of precision metrology and not a new phenomenon. Support is also concentrated among the atomic-physics members and I am outside that specialty, so my confidence in the fine priority questions (other early lattice-clock proposers, Takamoto's early demonstrations, theory of shifts) rests on colleagues. The three-person limit leaves no room for a third clock name, so the citation must be drafted narrowly around the lattice concept and its realisation.

responses.point: Ulf ranks topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect first as a deep conceptual discovery with a clear before and after, confirmed by many groups, while acknowledging that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang are missing and that Hasan's 3D work is left out.
responses.response: I take the scientific case seriously and I ranked B004 fourth myself. But my reservation is the one you name: the HgTe proposal by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang cannot be reflected in the supplied names, and Hasan's 3D work is a separate strong claim. A prize that gives Kane, Mele and Molenkamp the credit while leaving out the proposers of the very experiment Molenkamp ran is the sort of attribution problem I would not want to defend. It also follows the 2016 topological prize more closely than lattice clocks follow 2005 and 2012. Lattice clocks have no comparable hole in the credited list, so I keep them ahead, though I will not argue B004 is unworthy.

responses.point: Goran ranks circuit QED first as a clean, foundational demonstration that supplies the readout and coupling architecture of every superconducting processor, and flags his own closeness to credited people and the Chalmers community.
responses.response: I agree circuit QED is foundational and mature. I disagree on timing and attribution. The 2025 prize went to macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits, which is very close in theme, and I would be uneasy returning to that platform so soon. The four-name list also forces the choice between Girvin and Blais that you and Eva Olsson resolved differently, and I cannot see an obviously fairer trio. Because you state a possible conflict on this candidate, I would ask that you do not lead the committee's discussion of it, though I value your technical input on what was decisive. If the committee prefers quantum devices, I would like to hear whether you see lattice clocks as comparably decisive.

responses.point: Olle ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first, pairing the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction with the Jarillo-Herrero experiments, and notes that the superconducting pairing mechanism is unsettled and that Bistritzer's omission from a two-person prize would be a real cost.
responses.response: The theory-then-experiment story is compelling, and the speed of independent reproduction is impressive. Where I differ is maturity. You yourself list the pairing mechanism as unresolved, and Bernhard and Eva Olsson also call the recognition somewhat early. For an instrument-oriented judge, the lattice clock has a long record of comparisons between independent laboratories with agreeing numbers, while twisted bilayer graphene has a recent and still moving interpretation, and a credit question about Bistritzer and the Cao experimental work. I would not rule out B017 in a few years, but I think we should be wary of rewarding it now. I would be willing to hear a case that it is mature enough as a discovery of the phases, independent of the mechanism.

responses.point: Bernhard ranks the KTHNY theory of two-dimensional melting first as a clean, analytically controlled mechanism with decades of confirmation in colloids and related systems, with credit going to Halperin, Nelson and Young.
responses.response: The maturity is not in doubt, and I respect a prize for a simple mechanism with universal exponents. My reservation is overlap and fit. You note yourself that the 2016 prize for topological defects and phase transitions may have covered the central insight, and that some real systems melt through first-order transitions. I am also outside the field and cannot judge which experiments were decisive. Since only you ranked it, I do not see it as a consensus candidate yet. If you can show that the hexatic phase was clearly confirmed experimentally and that the 2016 citation did not cover it, I would reconsider it as a possible second part of the prize with a lattice-clock part, but the name limit would then be a problem.

responses.point: Stefan ranks lattice clocks first and atom interferometry second, treating both as measurement advances that expand what can be observed, and he notes that credit among Bordé, Pritchard, Kasevich and others for atom interferometry is contested.
responses.response: I agree on lattice clocks and share your view that the credit is adequate. On atom interferometry I am less convinced than you are. I ranked it seventh. The method is mature and useful, but the credit is contested (Chu, Mlynek and Keith, among others) and Chu already holds a prize for the underlying cooling. I do not think it should accompany lattice clocks as a second part, and a prize built from two measurement techniques would also strain the three-person limit. Unlike you, I would keep B034 off the preferred configuration unless you can argue that the supplied trio is the fairest.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Whether other early lattice-clock proposers or early demonstrators should have been credited alongside Katori and Ye, which the supplied names cannot settle.
Whether IceCube (B029) or the gamma-ray burst afterglows (B011) can be given a defensible three-person credit list, since both remain my fallbacks for a prize with an astronomical window.
How much weight the committee gives to the 2025 superconducting-circuit prize when judging circuit QED and optomechanics.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B041 (lattice clocks), B004, B017, B027, B028 or the atomic and quantum-information candidates. I work in the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations and in the same astroparticle community as IceCube and gamma-ray burst work (B029, B011), but I have no personal or institutional tie to the credited individuals that would require recusal. As Chair I am also treating my own opening ranking as one view among eight.
